What a key change is, and what it changes
  • Half steps. A half step is the smallest step on a piano, one key to the very next. Twelve half steps make an octave. Moving a whole song up or down by half steps is called transposing, or changing its key.
  • Tone 3 is a pattern, not a pitch. In Byzantine and Syriac chant a tone (echos in Greek, qolo in Syriac) is the shape of the scale, its strong notes and its melodic formulas, all measured from its base note. The chanter chooses the actual starting pitch to suit his voice or the choir, so the same Tone 3 can start on any note. Moving the song keeps every step, every in-between note and every turn exactly the same distance apart; the whole song simply sits higher or lower.
  • Everything follows. Learn a song, Master a song, Daily practice, the Song scale lessons, the singer under the voice basics, and this song's course in the Songs tab all use the new key. Your progress stays, because it is kept by note and phrase, not by pitch. Note names follow the key: if he sings G♯ and you move down 2, you sing F♯.
  • His voice, moved naturally. The app finds each pulse of his voice and moves the pulses closer together (higher) or further apart (lower) without changing their shape. His vowels and the color of his voice stay his and only the pitch moves, so there is no slowed-tape or cartoon sound. Breaths and consonants stay exactly as recorded, and the timing never changes. It is prepared once per key and kept on this device.
  • Which key to pick. If his high notes strain your voice, or his low notes go breathy, move the song toward the middle of your voice: "Fit my voice" finds the smallest move that does it. If it already feels comfortable, learning it as sung is the most exact and lets you sing along with him note for note. You can always come back.

    Daily practice

    KeyAs sung

    How daily practice works
    • Warm-up, 2 to 5 minutes. Lip trill or straw on home, sirens up a fifth and back, home on "ah", and an easy sweep through your range. Half-closed-mouth sounds (trill, straw, hum) make the voice start with less pressure, which is why they come first.
    • Voice basics. The two to four units that need you most (least practiced, longest ago, or marked hard), a few drills from each, mixed together rather than one unit at a time. Each unit picks up where it left off, so over a week you cover whole rounds.
    • The song. The Master a song program with the rest of the time: due reviews, new material, a hard spot, joins, memory work, and a finish from memory over the ison.
    • Voice rests. In sessions of 30 minutes or more, every 20 minutes the singing stops for about a minute and a half and you just listen to the singer. Listening to the model is not wasted time: it helps learning and overnight consolidation.
    • The mix follows your year. Phase 1 Foundation is mostly voice basics; by Phase 4 Mastery most of the time is the song. The slider nudges it either way.
    • Rating. After a session, "That session felt" moves the pace a step, and marks the units practiced as needing more or less time.
    • Hum first, words later. In the song, new pieces are hummed; words come in once a phrase is at the reviewing stage, because singing on a syllable is measurably more accurate than singing with lyrics.
    • Headphone use. The lock screen shows the current drill. Headphone buttons: play or pause; double-tap next drill; triple-tap repeat.
    • Your voice. Hum and sing at an easy, speaking-level volume, never pushed. If your voice feels tired, scratchy or hoarse, stop for the day: that is fatigue, and it recovers with rest, not with more practice. Water helps.
    Why it is built this way (the research)
    • Leaps. People who sing off pitch mostly hear fine; they shrink big jumps when they sing them (Pfordresher and Brown, 2007), and isolated intervals are the weakest task of all for untrained singers (Berkowska and Dalla Bella, 2013). So leaps are slid into first, then jumped cleanly from home, then sung from memory.
    • Patterns. Short melodies by ear are what singing a song is made of; random-order practice holds up better at a later test than drilling one thing (Stambaugh, 2011). Vivid auditory imagery goes with accurate singing (Pfordresher and Halpern, 2013), hence the think-it-first rounds.
    • Tuning ear. Non-musicians' pitch discrimination reached musicians' level after roughly 4 to 8 hours of training (Micheyl, Delhommeau, Perrot and Oxenham, 2006). The beats between two close tones are the cue every lock in this app relies on; this unit teaches you to hear them on purpose.
    • Warm-up. Semi-occluded vocal tract exercises (straw, lip trill, humming) lower the pressure needed to start the voice and make it more efficient (Titze, 2006); five to ten minutes of warm-up is enough to begin, with no gain from fifteen (University of Miami Miller School).
    • Voice rest. Two hours of continuous voice use produces fatigue that takes hours to recover from (Hunter and Titze, 2009). Long sessions here are split with rests, and the four-part drills already leave you silent about a third of the time.
    • Model listening. Musicians who heard a recording of the target before practicing learned faster and kept more overnight (Cash, Allen, Simmons and Duke, 2014).
    • Human voice. Matching a human voice is easier than matching a synthetic tone for many singers (Hutchins and Peretz, 2012), so the singer's held notes play under the tones in the basics too.
    • Every day. Adults who stop singing lose accuracy: "use it or lose it" (Demorest and Pfordresher, 2015); practice, not talent, predicted who improved. Precision (hitting the same note the same way each time) matters as much as accuracy (Pfordresher, Brown, Meier, Belyk and Liotti, 2010), hence the three-times-from-memory drills.
    • Syllable before words. Singing on a syllable produced fewer interval errors than singing with lyrics (Berkowska and Dalla Bella, 2013).

    How it works

      Your song

      KeyAs sung

      Psalm 23 is built in. Its recording is stored locked, because the app is a public website and the recording is not yours to share. Enter your passphrase once in this browser to unlock the singer.

      How the song lesson works
      • The singer underneath. Every time a tone plays, the real singer plays under it at the volume you pick below (1 to 10), slowed to the same timing without changing pitch. On held notes the singer's vowel is held steady with the tone. "On your own" is always silent, so you find out what you can do alone.
      • 1. The notes in this part. Each different note, by name, held and locked one at a time.
      • 2. The moves. Every move between two notes in the part, named and sized: "D, up a whole step, E".
      • 3. Piece by piece. Three or four notes at a time, slowly, then pieces joined together.
      • 4. The whole part, slowly.
      • Tone pitch. "Nearest note" rounds each note to the closest half step in the singer's own key, a clean target to lock onto. "Exactly as the singer sings" plays his real pitch, including notes that sit between Western notes. The notes list shows how far those are, in cents (100 cents is a half step).
      • The turns. Inside many words the singer moves quickly up and down around the main note. With "Add the turns" on, each piece is followed by the same piece with every turn, slower, and the whole part is sung once with the turns. Learn the main notes first, then add the turns.
      • 5. With the recording. The real singer at full volume and real speed: listen, sing along, sing it alone, then check.
      • Longer sessions go deeper. When there is time, the lesson adds: pieces in mixed order (find each start note fresh), think it then sing it (hear it, imagine it in silence, then sing it alone), hold the long notes, and the whole part closer to real speed. Short sessions keep the core steps.
      • As your minutes on this part grow (level 2 after 20 minutes, level 3 after 50), the early steps shrink and the tempo moves closer to the real song. Then move the part forward to the next phrase.
      • The parts come from the pauses the app finds in the recording, so pick the From and To that match what you hear.

      The singer's scale

      Focus for the next session

      Next session
        How Master a song works
        • The song map. The whole recording is measured once. Every main note gets the singer's exact pitch. His notes cluster into his own scale (some of them sit between Western notes), and the app lists every move between two of his notes, every melodic formula that comes back (chant melodies reuse formulas, many of them cadences that close a phrase), the turns inside words, and the hard spots: big leaps, in-between notes, quick notes, dense turns and rare notes.
        • Just in time. Before each new phrase you meet the notes it needs over the ison, its tricky moves, and any formula that starts there. Then the phrase itself (in pieces, then whole), then its hard spot. A new phrase only opens when no more than one other is still settling, so depth comes before breadth.
        • Spaced and mixed. Everything you have met comes back on a schedule: about 10 hours, then 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days. Reviews are mixed together instead of grouped, which feels harder but sticks better.
        • Support fades. New: slow, with the singer and the tone, several times. Learning: one pass, then on your own. Reviewing: real speed, then only the first note and you sing the rest from memory. Mastered: from memory, checked against the singer alone. Never faster than the singer.
        • Hard spots, deliberately. Zoom in on the hardest move, the window slowly, then with one note before and after, then from memory at real speed.
        • Memory work. Start anywhere (a random phrase from its first note), fill the gap (the singer drops out for one phrase in the middle), everything so far, and every session ends from memory over the ison.
        • Fine detail. "Which is the singer's note?" plays his in-between note and the nearest Western note; then you sing his. Phrases with every turn come in once the main notes are settled.
        • Your ratings. After a session, tap what felt shaky or easy. During a session, "This one felt shaky" marks the current drill.
        • Tone pitch. "The singer's scale" plays each note at the pitch he uses for that step on average, so the same note is always the same pitch. "Exactly as sung" follows each note as he sang it that time. "Nearest Western note" rounds to the closest half step in his key.
        The research behind it
        • Most people who sing off pitch hear pitch fine; the trouble is turning a heard pitch into the right vocal action, and they tend to shrink big leaps (Pfordresher and Brown, 2007). So the program is mostly singing, with big moves isolated, and only a little listening quiz.
        • Poor-pitch singers imagine melodies less vividly (Pfordresher and Halpern, 2013), so there are think-it, first-note-only and from-memory steps.
        • A real voice is easier to match than a synthetic tone for many singers (Hutchins and Peretz, 2012), which is why the singer plays under the tones.
        • Next-day results tracked how accurately pianists practiced and how they handled errors, not how long they practiced (Duke, Simmons and Cash, 2009): hence the hard-spot zoom and the shaky marks.
        • Random-order practice held up better at a later retention test than blocked practice in beginning clarinetists (Stambaugh, 2011), and learners tend to wrongly believe fixed order works better (Abushanab and Bishara, 2013). Music-learning labs also find skills keep consolidating between sessions and overnight, which is why the program spreads each piece over days.
        • Practicing from memory early (retrieval) showed a consistent but not yet statistically solid advantage after two days in a recent piano study (Benitez), so memory steps are included without overselling them.
        • Singers who memorize fastest learn in sections, link them progressively, monitor their mistakes, and practice from memory early; landmarks let you start anywhere (Ginsborg; Chaffin).
        • Syriac chant is an oral tradition, heavily ornamented and with intervals outside Western tuning, which is why the program learns the singer's own scale and turns rather than rounding them away.
        Sound and voice
        Background prepares the whole session first (a few seconds) and uses a recorded voice for short cues. Step by step speaks every instruction in full but stops if you leave the page.

        How to practice this way, and at work
        • Hear the lock. When your hum and the tone are a little apart you hear a slow wobble, a "wah-wah" called beating. The closer you get, the slower it wobbles; when it stops, you are in tune. Hum rather than sing words: it is much easier to hear.
        • Slide slowly. If you hear beating, move your pitch very slowly up or down. If the wobble gets faster, go the other way.
        • Feel it too. In a loud shop you may hear yourself mostly inside your head. Notice the buzz in your face and chest when you lock in; that feeling becomes your memory of the note.
        • Safety first. Keep your hearing protection. Use protective headphones or isolating earbuds with sound, and never turn the tone up to compete with a saw. Pause before any cut that needs your full attention: one press on the headphone button.
        • Short and often. Your voice learns best in regular sessions of 10 to 30 minutes with breaks, not one long one. Sip water.
        • Switch tabs or lock the phone. With the Background engine (the default) the whole session is prepared as one sound track before it starts, so it keeps playing in another tab, another app, or with the screen locked. Pause, skip and repeat from the lock screen or your headphone button. The step-by-step engines speak every instruction in full but need this page open with the screen on.
        • The order. Start with Unit 0 until locking onto home feels natural, then 1, 2 and 3. Each unit shows a time goal; the level rises as your minutes grow. Use the Note explorer any time, and come back to the screen lessons now and then to see your real scores.

        Byzantine scale workout

        A complete warm-up and practice on the Byzantine scale, built on your home note. It moves from straw and hum work, to the two half steps and the wide step, to the open voice, to patterns, to the whole scale over the ison and in chant tuning, then a phrase and the scale from memory. It gets a little faster and stricter every few workouts.

        Time I have

        Today's routine

          Why it is built this way
          • Straw and hum first. Semi-occluded singing (straw, lip trill, hum) makes the folds vibrate with less effort; a few minutes of straw work measurably eased voices in a 2013 study (Guzman et al.), and it is the standard opener in voice science (Titze).
          • Small before wide. The scale is learned the way Byzantine theory teaches it: by tetrachords (four-note halves), and inside them interval by interval, so the half steps and the wide step are each solid before the full octave.
          • Middle voice before range. Everything starts on your home note and widens gradually, low effort first.
          • Patterns. Groups of three and broken thirds make you hear every corner of the scale, not just the run up and down.
          • Over the ison. Singing against a held tonic exposes small tuning errors as a slow wobble, which is why chanters and string players practice with a drone.
          • From memory last. Taking the guide away tests the inner ear, after the scale is warm.

          Habits

          The coach reads the shape of your pitch line on every note: how it starts, holds, ends and moves, how phrases drift, how your high and low notes behave, and how you do without the guide. Only patterns that keep coming back across sessions show up here, most important first. Each one has a short fix-it drill.

          Nothing consistent yet. Keep practicing: after a few sessions, any recurring habits will appear here with drills to fix them.

                Challenge

                A session works through lessons in order from the one you pick. Sessions of 10 minutes or more open with a gentle straw or lip-trill warm-up, and 15 minutes or more end with a cool-down. Older lessons come back as review, weakest first. If the unit runs out before your time does, you get extra practice on its weakest lessons. A lesson is complete at 70 or better. Each unit ends with a test that touches every lesson's hardest exercise: score 90 to master the unit. Each unit also has a practice-time goal based on about 20 minutes a day, 5 days a week; every minute you actually sing counts toward goals and your rank, so extra practice moves you along faster. Exercises with an ison or a second voice work best with headphones. Everything stays open, so you can go back or jump ahead.
